t.1.3.1: Sūta said: Janamejaya, son of Parikṣit, was attending a long sacrificial session at Kurukṣetra together with his brothers. His three brothers were Śrutasena, Ugrasena, and Bhīmasena.
t.1.3.2: While they were sitting at that sacrificial session, a dog, the son of Saramā, came there. Beaten by Janamejaya's brothers, he went howling again and again to his mother.
t.1.3.3: His mother said to him as he wailed loudly, "Why are you crying? By whom have you been struck?"
t.1.3.4: Thus addressed, he replied to his mother, "I have been struck by the brothers of Janamejaya."
t.1.3.5: His mother replied to him, "Clearly you must have committed some offense there, because of which you were beaten."
t.1.3.7: Hearing that, his mother Saramā, stricken with grief for her son, came to that sacrificial session where Janamejaya, together with his brothers, was engaged in the long sacrifice.
t.1.3.6: He said to her again: "I have done no wrong at all. I do not look at the oblations, nor do I lick them."
t.1.3.8: There the angry bitch said to him, "This son of mine does no wrong at all; why has he been beaten?" And since he has been beaten though he did no harm, an unforeseen danger shall therefore come upon you."
t.1.3.9: Thus addressed by Saramā, the bitch of the gods, Janamejaya was greatly alarmed and dejected.
t.1.3.10: When that sacrificial session was completed, he returned to Hāstinapura and, seeking a suitable house priest, made the utmost effort, thinking, "Who might appease the evil spell that has come upon me?"
t.1.3.11: Once, Janamejaya, the son of Parikṣit, having gone out hunting, saw a hermitage in a certain region of his own kingdom.
t.1.3.12: There dwelt a certain seer named Śrutaśravā. He had a beloved son, named Somaśravā.
t.1.3.13: Janamejaya Pārikṣita approached that son of his and chose him for the office of family priest.
t.1.3.14: Having paid homage to that seer, he said, "Blessed one, let this son of yours be my family priest."
t.1.3.15: Thus addressed, he replied: "Janamejaya, this son of mine, born of a she-serpent, is a great ascetic, accomplished in Vedic study, sustained by the power of my austerities, and grown in the womb of her who drank my seed; he is able to quell all your evil afflictions except one wrought by Mahādeva. But he has one secret vow: should any brahmin ask him for anything, he must give it to him. If you can accept this, then take him."
t.1.3.17: Taking that purohita with him, he returned and said to his brothers, "This man has been chosen by me as our teacher; whatever he may say must be done by you without hesitation."
t.1.3.16: Thus addressed by him, Janamejaya replied to him, "Blessed one, it shall be so."
t.1.3.18: Thus addressed by him, his brothers did as he said. Having thus instructed his brothers, he set out against Takṣaśilā and brought that country under his control.
t.1.3.19: Meanwhile there was a certain seer named Dhaumya Āyoda. He had three disciples: Upamanyu, Āruṇi, and Veda.
t.1.3.20: He sent one of his disciples, Āruṇi of Pāñcāla, saying, "Go and bind up the breach in the field's dike."
t.1.3.21: Instructed by his teacher, Āruṇi Pāñcālya went there, but he was unable to dam that breach in the field's embankment.
t.1.3.22: Struggling in distress, he saw a way and thought, "So be it, I shall do this."
t.1.3.23: He lay down there in the breach of the field-dike, and while he lay there, that water stood still.
t.1.3.24: Then one day the teacher Āyoda Dhaumya asked his pupils, "Where has Āruṇi of Pāñcāla gone?"
t.1.3.26: Thus addressed, he replied to those disciples, "Then let us all go to the place where he is."
t.1.3.25: They replied, "He was sent by you yourself, revered sir, with the words, 'Go, dam up the breach in the field.'"
t.1.3.27: Going there, he called out to summon him: "Ho, Āruṇi of Pāñcāla, where are you? Come, my son!"
t.1.3.28: Hearing his teacher's words, Āruṇi rose at once from that breach in the field-dike, approached his teacher and said to him: "Here I am; I had lain down in the breach of the dike to stop the escaping water that could not otherwise be held back, and on hearing your voice, Lord, I at once broke through the dike and have come before you. I salute you, Lord; let your honour command me: what shall I do?"
t.1.3.29: The teacher said to him, "Since you have risen up after breaking through the embankment of the field, you shall therefore be known by the name Uddālaka."
t.1.3.30: He was blessed by his teacher: "Since you have carried out my word, you will attain the highest good. All the Vedas will shine forth to you, and all the treatises on dharma as well."
t.1.3.31: Thus addressed by his teacher, he went to the desired place.
t.1.3.32: Now that same Āyoda Dhaumya had another disciple, Upamanyu by name.
t.1.3.33: The teacher sent him off, saying, "Dear child Upamanyu, guard the cows."
t.1.3.34: At his teacher's word, he guarded the cows. Having guarded the cows by day, at the close of the day he returned, stood before his teacher, and bowed to him.
t.1.3.35: The teacher saw that he was fat, and he said to him, "My child Upamanyu, by what means do you sustain your livelihood? You are very fat."
t.1.3.36: He replied to his teacher, "I make my living by begging alms."
t.1.3.37: The teacher replied to him, "The alms you receive by begging must not be used without first offering them to me."
t.1.3.38: Saying "So be it," he again tended the cows; and having tended them, he returned and, standing before his teacher just as before, paid him homage.
t.1.3.39: Seeing him still just as stout, the teacher said to him, "Upamanyu, my child, I take all of your alms, leaving nothing. How do you support yourself now?"
t.1.3.41: The teacher replied to him: "This is not proper conduct toward a guru. By behaving thus you obstruct the livelihood of others as well; you are greedy."
t.1.3.40: Thus addressed by his teacher, he replied: "Having first offered the alms to you, my lord, I go begging again, and with that I sustain my living."
t.1.3.42: Saying "So be it," he guarded the cows. And having guarded them, he came back to his teacher's house, stood before his teacher, and bowed to him.
t.1.3.43: Seeing him still fat all the same, the teacher spoke to him again: "I take all your alms, and you do not go begging for anything else, yet you are fat. By what means do you make your living?"
t.1.3.44: He replied to his teacher, "Sir, I sustain my livelihood on the milk of these cows."
t.1.3.45: The teacher replied to him, "It is not proper for you to consume this milk, which I have not permitted."
t.1.3.46: Promising, "So be it," he guarded the cows, and then, returning again to his teacher's house, he stood before his guru and bowed in reverence.
t.1.3.47: The teacher saw him still fat, and said to him: "You do not eat the alms, nor do you go begging for more, nor do you drink milk, yet you are fat; by what means do you sustain your livelihood?"
t.1.3.48: Thus addressed, he replied to his teacher: "Sir, I drink the foam that these calves spit up as they suck at their mothers' udders."
t.1.3.49: The teacher replied to him: "Out of compassion for you, these virtuous calves spit out a great deal of foam. So by living in this way you obstruct the calves' livelihood; you ought not to drink even the foam."
t.1.3.50: Promising, "So be it," he guarded those cows without food. Thus forbidden, he does not eat alms, nor does he go begging for anything else; he does not drink milk, nor does he make use of the froth.
t.1.3.51: Once, in the forest, tormented by hunger, he ate the leaves of the arka plant.
t.1.3.52: Struck in his eyes by those arka leaves he had eaten, which were acrid, pungent and hot in their digestion, he became blind. And though blind, he kept wandering about, and he fell into a well.
t.1.3.53: Then, when he did not come, the teacher said to his pupils, "Upamanyu has been forbidden by me in every way; he is surely angry, and so he does not come, though he has been gone a long time."
t.1.3.54: Having spoken thus, he went into the forest and called out for Upamanyu: "Ho, Upamanyu, where are you? Come, my child!"
t.1.3.55: Hearing that call from his teacher, he answered loudly, "Here I am, O teacher, fallen into the well!"
t.1.3.56: The teacher replied to him, "How is it that you have fallen into a well?"
t.1.3.57: He replied to him, "Having eaten arka leaves, I have become blind; that is why I fell into the well."
t.1.3.58: The teacher replied to him, "Praise the Aśvins; those two physicians of the gods will make you sighted."
t.1.3.59: Thus addressed by his teacher, he began to praise the two gods, the Aśvins, with words of the Ṛg verses.
t.1.3.60: With my voice I praise you two who go before, the firstborn, of brilliant radiance, blazing and endless, the two divine fair-winged birds, free of dust, the two celestial chariots that dwell above all the worlds.
t.1.3.61: I praise the two golden birds, the guides to the world beyond, Nāsatya and Dasra, fair-nosed and victorious, who swiftly weave the bright white thread with their fine looms and weave across it the black and the shining.
t.1.3.63: Three hundred and sixty milch cows bear a single calf, and they milk it; kept in separate pens yet having a single milking, those two Aśvins milk out the hot oblation worthy of hymns.
t.1.3.62: The quail that had been seized by the might of the eagle, the Aśvins set free for her good fortune. Then, through magic power, they bowed before the two of excellent conduct and drove forth the finest ruddy cows.
t.1.3.64: Seven hundred spokes rest upon the one nave, and twenty other spokes are fixed in the felloes; the rimless wheel revolves, unaging, and the people anoint the two Aśvins of magic power.
t.1.3.65: A single wheel turns, with twelve spokes, a felly, six naves and one axle, the holder of the nectar of immortality, upon which all the gods are fastened; those two Aśvins set it loose. Do not falter, you two!
t.1.3.67: In the beginning you two bring forth the ten directions; at the summit your chariot-paths range alike through the skies. Along their course the seers follow, and gods and men move upon the earth.
t.1.3.68: You two fashion colors of every form, and they hold sway over all the worlds. Those rays, too, move on as they are followed, and gods and men roam over the earth.
t.1.3.66: Let the two Aśvins, grown mighty, hide the amṛta from Indra; let the Aśvins conceal her whose lord was the Dāsa. Having split the mountain, the Aśvins drove forth the cow, she who had been renowned through the rain-pouring might of Vala.
t.1.3.71: Thus praised by him, the two Aśvins came and said to him: "We are pleased. Here is a cake for you; eat it."
t.1.3.70: Let the two youths conceive an embryo through the mouth; a lifeless one brings it forth by the forepart of the foot. The embryo, as soon as it is born, devours its mother; you two Aśvins release the cows so that they may live.
t.1.3.72: Thus addressed, he replied, "You two have not spoken an untruth, but I cannot bring myself to eat this cake without first offering it to my teacher."
t.1.3.73: Then the Aśvins said to him: "Formerly, when your teacher praised us in just this way, we were pleased and gave him a cake, and he ate it without offering it to his guru. You too must do just as your teacher did."
t.1.3.69: We invoke you two, the Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, and the lotus garland that you two wear. Immortal are those two Nāsatyas, who further the truth; apart from the gods, she brings that forth with the forepart of her foot.
t.1.3.74: Thus addressed, he replied to them once more: "I entreat you both, Aśvins, I dare not eat it without first offering it to my teacher."
t.1.3.76: Thus addressed by the Aśvins, he, having regained his sight, came into the presence of his teacher, saluted the teacher, and told him what had happened. And the teacher was pleased with him.
t.1.3.75: The two Aśvins, pleased, said to him: "We are delighted by this devotion of yours to your teacher. Your teacher's teeth are of black iron, but yours shall be of gold; you shall regain your sight and you shall attain the highest good."
t.1.3.78: This, too, was the test of that Upamanyu.
t.1.3.79: Now there was another disciple of that same Āyoda Dhaumya, named Veda.
t.1.3.80: The teacher instructed him: "Veda, my child, stay here. You must remain in my house for some time, rendering obedient service; good fortune will come to you."
t.1.3.82: After a long time his teacher became satisfied with him, and from that satisfaction he obtained the highest good and omniscience. This, too, was the trial of Veda.
t.1.3.85: Then, after some time, the two kṣatriyas Janamejaya and Pauṣya approached the brahmin Veda and chose him as their teacher.
t.1.3.86: Once, setting out on business for those for whom he performed sacrifices, he charged his disciple named Uttaṅka: "O Uttaṅka, whatever falls short in our house, I wish you to make it good so that nothing is lacking."
t.1.3.87: Having thus instructed Uttaṅka, Veda went away on a journey.
t.1.3.88: Then Uttaṅka, eager to serve his teacher and carrying out his teacher's command, lived there in his teacher's house.
t.1.3.90: Addressed thus, he replied to those women: "I must not do this improper thing at the word of women, for I have not been instructed by my teacher, 'You must do even what is improper.'"
t.1.3.89: While he was living there, the women of his teacher's household gathered together, summoned him and said: “Your teacher's wife is in her season, and the teacher is away from home. See to it that this season of hers does not pass fruitless, for she is grieving over this.”
t.1.3.91: After some time his teacher returned home from that journey, and when he learned in full what he had done, he was pleased.
t.1.3.92: And he said to him, "Dear Uttaṅka, what may I do that is pleasing to you? For you have served me in accordance with dharma, and thereby our affection for each other has grown. So I give you leave; you will attain every success. Go now."
t.1.3.93: Addressed in this way, he replied, "What can I do that would please you?" For thus they say:
t.1.3.94: He who would teach against the law, and he who asks against the law: of these two, one perishes and incurs enmity.
t.1.3.95: "Now that you have given me leave, I wish to bring you whatever you desire as the teacher's fee."
t.1.3.96: Thus addressed by him, the teacher replied, "My dear Uttaṅka, stay here for the time being."
t.1.3.97: One day Uttaṅka said to his teacher, "Let your honor command me: what pleasing thing shall I bring you as the teacher's fee?"
t.1.3.98: The teacher replied to him, "Dear Uttaṅka, you have urged me many times, saying, 'Let me bring something for my teacher's sake.' So go, enter the house, and ask your teacher's wife here, 'What shall I bring?' Whatever she tells you, bring that."
t.1.3.77: And he said to him, "Just as the Aśvins said, so shall you attain what is best, and all the Vedas shall become manifest to you."
t.1.3.81: Saying "So be it," he dwelt for a long time in his teacher's house, devoted to serving his teacher. Like an ox ever yoked to heavy burdens, he endured cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and every hardship, and was never contrary in anything.
t.1.3.101: Thus addressed by his teacher's wife, Uttaṅka set out. As he went along the road, he saw a bull of enormous size, and mounted upon it a man, likewise of enormous size.
t.1.3.102: That man addressed Uttaṅka: "Uttaṅka, eat this dung of this bull!"
t.1.3.103: Thus addressed, he did not wish to do so.
t.1.3.100: Thus addressed, the teacher's wife replied to Uttaṅka: "Go to King Pauṣya, beg from him the two earrings worn by his kṣatriya queen, and bring them here. Four days from now there will be a holy festival, and I wish to serve the brāhmaṇas wearing them, so see to it that on that day I may shine with those earrings. For good fortune would be yours if you do me this favor."
t.1.3.104: The man said to him again, "Eat it, Uttaṅka, do not hesitate; your teacher too has eaten it before."
t.1.3.105: Thus addressed, Uttaṅka said, "Very well," and then, having eaten that dung and urine of the bull, he set out to where the Kṣatriya Pauṣya was.
t.1.3.99: Thus addressed by the teacher, he asked the teacher's wife: "It is so that I have been permitted by the teacher to go home, and so I wish to present the teacher's fee that you desire and depart free of debt. Therefore let your ladyship command me: what shall I bring as the teacher's fee?"
t.1.3.106: Uttaṅka approached him and saw him seated. Having approached him and greeted him with blessings, he said, "I have come to you as a petitioner."
t.1.3.107: Greeting him respectfully, he said, "Blessed one, I am indeed Pauṣya. What shall I do for you?"
t.1.3.108: Uttaṅka said to him: "I have come as a petitioner, in want of earrings for the sake of my teacher. The earrings that are worn by your kṣatriya wife, those you ought to give me."
t.1.3.109: Pauṣya replied to him: "Enter the inner apartments, and let the queen be asked."
t.1.3.110: Addressed thus by him, he entered the women's quarters but did not see the kṣatriya lady.
t.1.3.111: He said again to Pauṣya, "It is not fitting for you to treat us with falsehood. Your kṣatriya queen is not present in the inner apartments, for I do not see her."
t.1.3.84: He said nothing at all to his pupils, neither "Let work be done" nor "Let the teacher be served," for, knowing the hardships of dwelling in a teacher's house, he did not wish to burden his pupils with suffering.
t.1.3.112: Thus addressed, Pauṣya replied to him, "Right now you are in a state of impurity; just think back. For that kṣatriya lady cannot be seen by one who is impure or unclean; because of her devotion to her husband, she does not come into the sight of an unclean person."
t.1.3.83: Permitted by his teacher, he returned from that residence in his guru's house and entered the stage of the householder. While he too was living in his own house, three disciples came to him.
t.1.3.114: Pauṣya replied to him: "That is indeed so; ritual rinsing is not done by one who is walking, nor by one who is standing."
t.1.3.113: Thus addressed, Uttaṅka remembered and said, "It is true: I did rinse my mouth while still impure from eating, and while walking in haste."
t.1.3.115: Then Uttaṅka said, "So be it," and sat down facing east. Having thoroughly washed his hands, feet and face, he sipped noiseless water that reached down to his heart, drinking three times and wiping his mouth twice, and touched the openings of his senses with water. Then he entered the inner apartments and saw that Kṣatriya lady.
t.1.3.116: And as soon as she saw Uttaṅka, she rose, greeted him respectfully, and said, "Welcome to you, blessed one! Command me: what shall I do?"
t.1.3.117: He said to her: "Please give me these two earrings, which I have begged of you for the sake of my teacher."
t.1.3.118: Pleased by that true sincerity of his, and thinking, "This man is a worthy recipient and is not to be refused," she took off those two earrings and gave them to him.
t.1.3.119: And she said to him: "Takṣaka, the king of the Nāgas, covets these two earrings; you must carry them away with vigilance."
t.1.3.120: Thus addressed, he replied to that kṣatriya lady: "Lady, be entirely at ease; Takṣaka, the king of the Nāgas, is not able to harm me."
t.1.3.121: Having spoken thus, he took leave of that kṣatriya lady and came into the presence of Pauṣya.
t.1.3.122: Seeing him, he said, "Ho, Pauṣya, I am pleased."
t.1.3.124: Uttaṅka replied to him, "I am indeed in haste. I wish that food, such as is at hand, be quickly brought by you."
t.1.3.123: Pauṣya replied to him: “Blessed one, only after a long time is a worthy recipient found, and you are a virtuous guest. I shall perform that śrāddha; let a moment be granted.”
t.1.3.125: Saying "So be it," he fed him with such food as was at hand.
t.1.3.126: Then Uttaṅka, seeing that the food was cold and had a hair in it, and thinking it impure, said to Pauṣya: "Since you give me impure food, you shall therefore become blind."
t.1.3.127: Pauṣya replied to him: "Since you, too, defile food that is undefiled, you shall therefore be without offspring."
t.1.3.128: Then Pauṣya found out for himself that the food was indeed impure.
t.1.3.130: Uttaṅka replied to him: "I do not speak falsely. Having become blind, you will before long be no longer blind. May the curse given by you not fall upon me either."
t.1.3.129: Then, realizing that the food was impure because it had been brought by a woman with loosened hair and had hair in it, he sought to appease Uttaṅka: "Lord, it was out of ignorance that this food was served with hair in it and cold. I therefore beg your forgiveness; let me not become blind."
t.1.3.131: Pauṣya replied to him: "I am not able to take back the curse, for my anger has not subsided even now. And is this not known to you, how it is:
t.1.3.132: The heart of a brāhmaṇa is like fresh butter, but in his speech is set a razor with a sharp edge; for a kṣatriya both of these are the reverse: his speech is like butter, his heart sharp-edged.
t.1.3.133: "That being so, I am not able to make that curse otherwise, because of the sharpness of my heart. Let you be gone," thus he said.
t.1.3.135: Saying, "We shall accomplish it, then," Uttaṅka took those two earrings and set out.
t.1.3.134: Uttaṅka replied to him, "You appeased me only after you had found out that the food was impure. And earlier you said, 'Since you defile food that is not defiled, you shall be childless.' But since the food was in fact defiled, this curse shall not fall upon me."
t.1.3.136: On the road he saw a naked mendicant approaching, now visible, now invisible, again and again. Then Uttaṅka set those earrings down on the ground and went off in search of water.
t.1.3.137: Meanwhile that mendicant, hastening, came near, seized the two earrings and ran off. Uttaṅka ran after him and caught him. Then, abandoning that form and assuming the form of Takṣaka, he suddenly entered a great hole that lay open in the earth.
t.1.3.138: And having entered the world of the Nāgas, he went to his own dwelling. Uttaṅka followed him in through that very same hole, and having entered, he praised the Nāgas with these ślokas.
t.1.3.139: Those snakes whose king is Airāvata, splendid in battle, are like raining clouds driven onward by the wind and flashing with lightning.
t.1.3.140: Those born of Airāvata, some handsome and some misshapen, and wearing many-coloured earrings, shone like the sun on the vault of heaven.
t.1.3.141: Many are the paths of the Nāgas on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā; who but Airāvata would wish to roam amid the army of the sun's rays?
t.1.3.142: Twenty thousand and eight hundred and eighty serpents go along as his reins whenever Dhṛtarāṣṭra moves.
t.1.3.143: Those who approach him and those who have gone far away: to all these brothers, of whom Airāvata is the eldest, I have paid homage.
t.1.3.144: He whose dwelling was always in Kurukṣetra and in the Khāṇḍava forest, that son of Kadrū, Takṣaka, I have praised for the sake of the earrings.
t.1.3.145: Takṣaka and Aśvasena, the two ever-constant companions, dwelt in Kurukṣetra along the river Ikṣumatī.
t.1.3.147: Even though he praised the Nāgas in this way, when he still did not obtain the two earrings, he then saw two women weaving a cloth, having mounted it on a loom.
t.1.3.146: Takṣaka's younger brother, who is known by the name Śrutasena and who dwelt at Mahaddyumna aspiring to the chieftainship of the Nāgas, to that great-spirited one I shall always pay homage.
t.1.3.148: On that loom were black and white threads, and he saw a wheel being turned by six boys, and he saw a handsome man.
t.1.3.149: He praised them all with these ślokas spoken as sacred mantras.
t.1.3.150: Here three hundred and sixty spokes are fixed in the middle, and it moves ever onward on this steadfast wheel with its twenty-four joints, the wheel that six youths keep turning.
t.1.3.151: Two young women, ceaselessly turning the threads, weave this fabric of every form; spinning out the black threads and the white, they unceasingly bring forth beings and worlds.
t.1.3.152: He who bears the thunderbolt, protector of the world, slayer of Vṛtra and killer of Namuci, the great-souled one clad in two black garments, who separates truth from falsehood in the world.
t.1.3.154: Then that man said to him, "I am pleased with you for this hymn of praise. What favor may I do for you?"
t.1.3.153: He who has taken as his mount the stallion, the ancient embryo of the waters, Vaiśvānara: to him be homage always, to the lord of the universe, the lord of the three worlds, Puraṃdara.
t.1.3.155: He said to him, "May the Nāgas come under my power."
t.1.3.156: That man spoke to him again: "Blow into the anus of this horse."
t.1.3.157: He blew into the horse's anus. Then, as the horse was being blown into, smoky flames of fire burst forth from all its orifices.
t.1.3.159: Then Takṣaka, flustered and dejected by fear of the fire's blaze, took the two earrings, hastily came out of his abode and said to Uttaṅka, "Let your honor accept these two earrings."
t.1.3.158: By them the world of the Nāgas was filled with smoke.
t.1.3.161: Then, as he was still pondering, that man said to him: "Uttaṅka, mount this horse; it will bring you to your teacher's house in an instant."
t.1.3.160: Uttaṅka accepted them, and having received the earrings he reflected: “Today is that sacred observance of my teacher's wife, and I have come a long way; how indeed shall I manage to arrive in time?”
t.1.3.163: Then Uttaṅka entered and saluted the teacher's wife, and he gave her the two earrings.
t.1.3.162: Saying "So be it," he mounted that horse and returned to his teacher's house. The teacher's wife, having bathed, was sitting and having her hair dressed, and thinking, "Uttaṅka is not coming," she set her mind on cursing him.
t.1.3.165: Then Uttaṅka greeted his teacher respectfully, and the teacher replied to him, "Welcome, dear Uttaṅka! Why have you taken so long?"
t.1.3.164: And she replied to him: "Uttaṅka, you have come at the right place and the right time. Welcome to you, my child! Only narrowly have you escaped being cursed by me. Good fortune has come to you; may you attain success."
t.1.3.166: Uttaṅka replied to his teacher: "Sir, Takṣaka, the king of the Nāgas, put an obstacle in the way of this task, and by him I was taken to the world of the Nāgas."
t.1.3.167: And there I saw two women who had set a cloth upon a loom and were weaving it, and on that loom were black and white threads. What is that?
t.1.3.168: And there I saw a wheel with twelve spokes, and six boys were turning it round. What is that too?
t.1.3.169: And I also saw a man; who, then, was he?
t.1.3.171: As I was going along the road, I saw a bull, and a man was mounted on it; he addressed me courteously: "Uttaṅka, eat the dung of this bull; your teacher too has eaten it." Then, at his word, I ate the dung of that bull, and now I wish to be instructed by you: what was that?
t.1.3.170: And the horse of enormous size, who was he as well?
t.1.3.172: Addressed thus by him, the teacher replied: "Those two women are Dhātā and Vidhātā, and those black and white threads are night and day."
t.1.3.173: As for that twelve-spoked wheel which six youths were turning, they are the six seasons, and the wheel is the year. The man is Parjanya, and the horse is Agni.
t.1.3.174: The bull that you saw while going along the road was Airāvata, the king of the Nāgas, and the one who was mounted upon it was Indra. And the dung of that bull which you ate was the nectar of immortality.
t.1.3.175: It is because of that, indeed, that you did not perish in that abode of the Nāgas; and that Indra is also my friend.
t.1.3.177: Having been given leave by his teacher, Uttaṅka, enraged and wishing to take revenge on Takṣaka, set out for Hāstinapura.
t.1.3.176: By his grace you have obtained the earrings and come back again. So go, gentle one; I give you leave. You will attain what is good.
t.1.3.178: Having reached Hāstinapura before long, Uttaṅka, that best of twice-born men, went to meet King Janamejaya.
t.1.3.179: He saw him, the unconquered one, who had earlier returned from Takṣaśilā, wholly victorious and surrounded on all sides by his ministers.
t.1.3.180: Having first offered him blessings of victory in the proper manner, he then, at the right moment, addressed these words to him in a voice of perfect diction.
t.1.3.182: Thus addressed by the brahmin, King Janamejaya, his heart gladdened, duly honored that sage and replied.
t.1.3.181: While another task remains to be done, O best of kings, you, as if out of childishness, are doing something else entirely, O best of rulers.
t.1.3.183: By protecting these subjects I uphold my own duty as a kṣatriya. Or tell me, O best of brahmins, what is to be done; today I am eager to hear your words.
t.1.3.184: Thus addressed by the best of kings, that best of the twice-born, foremost among those who perform meritorious deeds, spoke to the king of undaunted spirit about his own purpose and about that which was the king's task as well.
t.1.3.185: O lord of the lords of men, take vengeance on that evil-souled serpent Takṣaka, by whom your father was slain.
t.1.3.187: For bitten by that wicked-souled one, the blameless king went to his death, like a tree struck by a thunderbolt.
t.1.3.186: I deem that the time has come for the deed that the ordinance prescribes; so go, O king, and requite the wrong done to that great-souled father of yours.
t.1.3.188: Puffed up with the arrogance of his strength, Takṣaka, that vilest of serpents, the evil one who bit your father, has done a deed that should never have been done.
t.1.3.189: That evildoer slew the king, the protector of the lineage of royal seers, who was like the immortals, and he also turned Kāśyapa back.
t.1.3.190: You ought to burn that wicked one in the blazing fire at a snake sacrifice, great king, for that duty rests upon you.
t.1.3.191: In this way you will have avenged your father, and a very great kindness will have been done to me, O king.
t.1.3.193: Having heard this, the king grew furious with Takṣaka, kindled by the oblation of Uttaṅka's words as a fire blazes up with an oblation.
t.1.3.192: O protector of the earth, O great king, O sinless one, it is that evil-souled one by whom an obstacle was placed in the way of my task while I was going about on my teacher's behalf.
t.1.3.194: Then the king, deeply grieved, questioned his own ministers, in the very presence of Uttaṅka, about his father's departure to heaven.
t.1.3.195: For at the very moment he heard from Uttaṅka what had befallen his father, that king of kings was overwhelmed with grief and sorrow.
